subject: maths
title: Mental strategies and number tricks
summary: Calculate quickly in your head by compensating, partitioning, doubling and halving, rearranging, and using number patterns such as (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b².
body:
Good mental maths is not about being a human calculator — it is about seeing a smarter path through a calculation. Shop owners totalling prices, builders working out quantities and anyone checking a bill use the same few tricks: round and adjust, break numbers apart, and rearrange to make easy pairs. In this lesson you will learn those tricks and, more importantly, *why* they work.

## Learning objective

By the end of this lesson you can choose and explain a mental strategy (compensating, partitioning, doubling and halving, rearranging or a "near a round number" trick) to calculate with whole numbers quickly and accurately.

## Before you start

This builds on **Adding and subtracting whole numbers (Year 7)**, **Multiplying and dividing whole numbers (Year 7)** and **Order of operations (BIDMAS) (Year 7)**.

Warm-up (answers below):

1. Work out 456 + 278.
2. Work out 36 × 7.

Answers: 1. 734  2. 252

## Think of it like this

### Paying with a round note

At a shop, something costs $19. Instead of counting out $19 in coins, you hand over a $20 note and get $1 change. You used an easy round number, then fixed it. That is exactly what **compensating** does: 19 × 6 is hard-ish, but 20 × 6 = 120, then take back the extra 6 to get 114.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* at the shop the "fix" is always a little change back. In maths the fix can be much bigger — when you multiply, the overshoot is multiplied too (20 × 6 overshoots by 1 × 6, not by 1).

## Key ideas

### Compensating: round, then adjust

**Compensating** means changing a number to a friendly one, calculating, then undoing the change.

- 297 + 486 = 300 + 486 − 3 = 786 − 3 = 783 (you added 3 too many, so take 3 away).
- 47 × 99 = 47 × 100 − 47 = 4700 − 47 = 4653 (99 lots of 47 is one lot fewer than 100 lots).

The fix has to match what you changed. When you multiply, you take away a whole *group*, not just 1.

### Partitioning and the distributive law

**Partitioning** means splitting a number into parts that are easy to work with. It works because of the **distributive law**: a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c.

- 6 × 98 = 6 × (100 − 2) = 600 − 12 = 588
- 53 × 11 = 53 × 10 + 53 = 530 + 53 = 583

**The ×11 shortcut for two-digit numbers:** write the two digits apart and put their sum in the middle. For 53 × 11: 5 _ 3 with 5 + 3 = 8 in the middle → 583. If the middle sum is 10 or more, carry: 87 × 11 → 8 (15) 7 → 957. It is just 87 × 10 + 87 written cleverly.

### Doubling and halving, and the "×5, ×25" tricks

If you double one number and halve the other, the product stays the same: 18 × 15 = 9 × 30 = 270.

- **× 5** is the same as × 10, then ÷ 2: 84 × 5 = 840 ÷ 2 = 420.
- **× 25** is the same as × 100, then ÷ 4: 36 × 25 = 3600 ÷ 4 = 900.

### Rearranging to make friendly pairs

Multiplication can be done in any order (the **commutative** and **associative laws**). Look for pairs that make 10, 100 or 1000: 4 × 25 = 100, 8 × 125 = 1000, 2 × 5 = 10.

- 4 × 37 × 25 = (4 × 25) × 37 = 100 × 37 = 3700

### Two numbers either side of a round number (a Year 8 idea)

When two numbers sit the same distance either side of a round number, multiply them like this:

(a + b) × (a − b) = a² − b²

So 43 × 37 = (40 + 3)(40 − 3) = 40² − 3² = 1600 − 9 = 1591. Why? Expanding gives 40 × 40 − 40 × 3 + 3 × 40 − 3 × 3; the middle two parts cancel out.

### Squaring numbers ending in 5

To square a number ending in 5, multiply the tens digit by the next number up, then write 25 on the end. 35²: 3 × 4 = 12 → 1225. 65²: 6 × 7 = 42 → 4225. (It works because 35² = 30 × 40 + 25, by the rule above with a = 35, b = 5.)

### Pairing to add a long list

To add 1 + 2 + 3 + … + 100, pair the first and last: 1 + 100, 2 + 99, 3 + 98 … each pair makes 101, and there are 50 pairs. Total = 50 × 101 = 5050.

## Worked examples

### Example 1

Work out 297 + 486 in your head.

Step 1: round 297 up to 300 — it is 3 away from a round number.
Step 2: 300 + 486 = 786 — easy with a round number.
Step 3: subtract the 3 you added: 786 − 3 = **783** — to undo the change.

Check: estimate 300 + 500 = 800, so 783 is sensible ✓

### Example 2

Work out 36 × 25.

Step 1: × 25 is the same as × 100 then ÷ 4 — because 25 = 100 ÷ 4.
Step 2: 36 × 100 = 3600.
Step 3: 3600 ÷ 4 = **900**.

Check: 36 = 4 × 9, so 36 × 25 = 9 × (4 × 25) = 9 × 100 = 900 ✓

### Example 3

Work out 47 × 99.

Step 1: 99 = 100 − 1, so 47 × 99 means 100 lots of 47, take away 1 lot of 47 — distributive law.
Step 2: 47 × 100 = 4700.
Step 3: 4700 − 47 = **4653** — remove one whole 47, not just 1.

Check: 47 × 99 should be a bit under 4700 ✓

### Example 4

Work out 43 × 37 without written working.

Step 1: notice 43 and 37 are both 3 away from 40 — so use (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b².
Step 2: 40² = 1600 and 3² = 9.
Step 3: 1600 − 9 = **1591**.

Check: the last digit of 3 × 7 = 21 is 1, and 1591 ends in 1 ✓

### Example 5

Add 1 + 2 + 3 + … + 20.

Step 1: pair first and last: 1 + 20 = 21, 2 + 19 = 21, … — every pair is the same.
Step 2: there are 20 numbers, so 10 pairs.
Step 3: 10 × 21 = **210**.

## Common mistakes

- **Fixing by the wrong amount after multiplying.** 47 × 99 is not 4700 − 1. Why: thinking about adding instead of multiplying. Fix: ask "how many *groups* did I add?" — here one group of 47.
- **Adjusting in the wrong direction.** If you rounded *up*, you must take away; if you rounded down, add back. Fix: say "I added 3 too many, so take 3 off."
- **Using a² − b² when the numbers aren't balanced.** 52 × 47 is not 50² − something, because 52 is 2 above 50 but 47 is 3 below. Fix: only use it when both are the same distance from the round number.
- **Forgetting to carry in the ×11 trick.** 87 × 11 is not 8157. Fix: if the middle sum is 10 or more, carry the 1 into the front digit.
- **Halving both numbers.** 18 × 15 is not 9 × 7.5 — halving both gives a quarter of the answer. Fix: halve one number and double the *other*: 9 × 30.

## Tips to remember

- **"Round it, then pay it back."** (A made-up memory trick.) Whatever you add to make it friendly, pay back at the end — and when multiplying, pay back a whole group.
- **Money pictures:** × 5 is "ten lots then half"; × 25 is "quarters — four make 100".
- **Look for 4 × 25 and 8 × 125** — they turn into 100 and 1000.
- **Same distance, square minus square:** 43 × 37, 52 × 48 and 61 × 59 are all "square of the middle, minus square of the gap".
- **Check with the last digit:** the last digit of the answer must match the last digit of (last digit × last digit).

## Key terms

- **Compensating** — changing a number to a friendly one, calculating, then adjusting to undo the change.
- **Partitioning** — splitting a number into parts that are easier to work with.
- **Distributive law** — a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c; multiplying a sum part by part.
- **Commutative law** — you can swap the order: a × b = b × a (also for adding).
- **Associative law** — you can regroup: (a × b) × c = a × (b × c) (also for adding).

## Summary

- Round to a friendly number, calculate, then adjust — when multiplying, adjust by a whole group.
- Split numbers using the distributive law: 6 × 98 = 600 − 12.
- × 5 = × 10 ÷ 2 and × 25 = × 100 ÷ 4; doubling one factor and halving the other keeps the product.
- Rearrange to make 100 or 1000, e.g. 4 × 25 and 8 × 125.
- Numbers balanced around a round number: (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b².

questions.prompt: Use the × 11 shortcut to work out 64 × 11.
questions.explanation: 6 + 4 = 10 goes in the middle, so carry: 6 (10) 4 becomes 704. 6104 forgets to carry.
steps: The middle is 6 + 4 = 10, which is 10 or more, so carry the 1 into the 6.

mistakes.B: Step 3: when the middle sum is 10 or more, carry the 1 — do not write both digits.
mistakes.C: Step 1: that is only 64 × 10. × 11 is × 10 plus one more 64.
mistakes.D: Step 2: the middle sum is 10 — you cannot write just the 1. Put 0 in the middle and carry the 1 into the 6.

questions.explanation: Rearrange: 4 × 25 = 100, then 100 × 37 = 3700. 925 is 37 × 25 with the 4 left out.
steps: You can multiply in any order, so pair 4 with 25.

mistakes.B: Step 1: you left out the 4 — that is only 37 × 25.

questions.prompt: 52 and 48 are both 2 away from 50. Use this to work out 52 × 48.
questions.explanation: (50 + 2)(50 − 2) = 50² − 2² = 2500 − 4 = 2496. 2016 comes from multiplying tens by tens and ones by ones only.
steps: Use (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b² with a = 50 and b = 2.

mistakes.C: Step 3: the rule is a² minus b², not plus.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 50 × 40 + 2 × 8 misses the cross parts (50 × 8 and 2 × 40). Use the a² − b² pattern.

questions.prompt: Work out 75² using the "ending in 5" trick.
questions.explanation: Tens digit 7 × the next number 8 = 56, then write 25: 5625. 4925 uses 7 × 7 instead of 7 × 8.
steps: Multiply the tens digit by the next number up: 7 × 8.

mistakes.A: Step 1: multiply 7 by the NEXT number up (8), not by itself.
mistakes.D: If you partitioned, you did 75 × 70 and forgot the 75 × 5 part.

questions.prompt: A school buys 98 concert tickets at $35 each. What is the total cost?
questions.explanation: 98 tickets is 100 tickets minus 2: 3500 − 2 × 35 = 3500 − 70 = 3430. $3465 takes off only one ticket.

mistakes.A: Step 2: you took off one ticket ($35), but 2 fewer tickets is $70.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 98 is fewer than 100, so subtract the $70.
mistakes.D: Step 3: you forgot to adjust — that is the cost of 100 tickets.

mistakes.B: Step 3: you forgot to take away 3².
